title: Wild Nature Shorts · Episode 1
chapters: Mangroves: forests at the edge of the sea

units.t: Wild Nature Shorts. Episode one.
In this episode: Mangroves: forests at the edge of the sea, Plants that eat animals and The hidden kingdom of fungi.
Part one. Mangroves: forests at the edge of the sea.
Muddy, smelly and buzzing with life, mangroves are trees that drink salt water, breathe through snorkels and quietly protect Australia's coasts.
Trees in the sea.
Walk a mangrove boardwalk at low tide and you hear snapping shrimp, popping air bubbles in the mud and crabs scuttling into holes.
Twice a day, the sea floods in over the roots.
Mangroves are not one kind of plant but a mix of trees and shrubs from different families, each adapted to life where land meets salt water.
They grow along sheltered tropical and warm coastlines worldwide.
Australia has around 40 species and one of the largest areas of mangrove forest of any country, across the north and down both the east and west coasts.
Around Darwin, Cairns and the Gulf of Carpentaria, they form vast, dense forests.
Salt, snorkels and stilts.
Salt water kills most plants by drawing water out of their cells.
Many mangroves filter salt out at the roots.
Others take it in and then expel it: the grey mangrove, Australia's most widespread species, pushes salt out through glands in its leaves, and you may taste crystals on a leaf's underside.
Some store salt in old leaves or bark and shed them.
This costs energy, so growth is often slower in very salty places.
Mangrove mud has almost no oxygen.
Grey mangroves send up pencil-like roots called pneumatophores that act as snorkels, taking in air through tiny pores at low tide.
Red mangroves stand on arching prop roots.
These tangles also anchor the trees and slow the water, so sediment settles and builds the shoreline.
Babies born ready.
Most plants drop seeds and wait for them to sprout.
Many mangroves do something closer to giving birth.
The seed germinates while still on the parent tree, growing into a seedling called a propagule.
In some species these look like long green cigars or pens dangling from the branches.
When ready, the propagule drops.
If the tide is out, it may lodge in the mud and start growing straight away.
If the tide is in, it floats off and can drift for weeks or even months before washing up somewhere suitable.
This head start helps the young plant establish where waves and tides would sweep away an ordinary seed.
It is also how mangroves have spread along coastlines and between islands across the tropics.
Nurseries and guardians.
Calm water and tangled roots make an ideal nursery.
Young fish and prawns hide from predators while feeding on fallen, decaying mangrove leaves.
Barramundi, mud crabs, mangrove jack and banana prawns all depend on mangroves for part of their lives.
Birds use them too.
The rotten egg smell is not a sign of trouble: it comes from bacteria breaking down organic matter in oxygen-poor mud, part of the recycling that makes the system so productive.
Mangroves also act as a natural sea wall, absorbing wave and storm surge energy.
Their waterlogged mud buries dead material, building deep, carbon-rich soil.
Per hectare, these 'blue carbon' ecosystems can store several times more carbon than many land forests.
Clearing them can release it.
Under pressure.
Worldwide, large areas of mangroves have been cleared for shrimp farms, ports, housing and farmland.
Australia's are in better shape than many, but not immune.
In late 2015 and early 2016, mangroves along roughly 1,000 kilometres of the Gulf of Carpentaria died back over a few months, affecting thousands of hectares.
Scientists linked the event to drought, high temperatures and a temporary drop in sea level during a strong El Niño.
Some areas have since begun to recover.
Mangroves are protected by law in Australian states and territories.
In Queensland, for example, they are protected marine plants, and damaging them without approval is an offence, so check local rules before trimming any.
The simplest way to appreciate them is from a boardwalk.
The key idea: Mangroves are a mix of salt-tolerant trees and shrubs that grow where tropical and warm coasts meet the tide.
Part two. Plants that eat animals.
Snapping traps, sticky tentacles and slippery pitchers: some plants have turned the tables on the animal world, and Australia is a hotspot for them.
Why eat meat.
Picture a peat bog: soggy, acidic and sunlit, with soil that holds almost no nitrogen or phosphorus.
Most plants struggle there.
Carnivorous plants thrive, because they trap and digest insects and other small creatures, absorbing the minerals the soil lacks.
They still make their own food from sunlight, like any green plant.
Prey is more of a fertiliser supplement than a main meal.
There are several hundred species, and the habit has evolved independently several times in unrelated plant groups, a sign of how useful it is in poor soils.
Each group came up with its own kind of trap, from snapping jaws to sticky glue to water-filled pits.
Flytraps and pitchers.
The Venus flytrap grows wild only in a small area of North and South Carolina.
Its trap is a pair of hinged lobes with a few trigger hairs.
One touch does nothing.
A second touch within about 20 seconds snaps it shut in a fraction of a second.
This counting stops the plant wasting energy on raindrops.
A struggling insect keeps brushing the hairs, which seals the trap and releases digestive juices.
Digestion takes several days, and each trap can open and close only a limited number of times.
Pitcher plants use a passive trap: a deep cup of digestive fluid with a slippery rim.
Insects tumble in and cannot climb out.
Australia has native Nepenthes pitcher plants in far north Queensland.
Sundews and bladderworts.
Sundews look covered in morning dew, but each tentacle's droplet is sticky glue.
A landing insect is held fast, and in many species the tentacles bend inward to press it against the leaf, where enzymes digest it.
Australia is one of the world's great centres of sundew diversity, especially the south-west of Western Australia.
Some are tiny pygmy sundews no bigger than a coin, and many survive dry summers as underground tubers.
Bladderworts, which live in water or wet soil, pump water out of tiny bladders to create low pressure.
When a water flea brushes a trigger hair, a trapdoor opens and the bladder sucks it in within a tiny fraction of a second, one of the fastest movements known in plants.
The Albany pitcher plant.
Australia has a true original: the Albany pitcher plant.
It grows wild only in a small coastal region of south-west Western Australia.
It is so distinctive that it is the only species in its plant family.
Its small, hairy pitchers sit at ground level, catching mostly ants and other crawling insects.
Plants like this are specialists of nutrient-poor wetlands and heaths, so they are vulnerable when those places change.
Draining swamps, clearing land, adding fertiliser and suppressing the natural fires that keep competing plants in check can all push them out.
Their striking looks also attract collectors, and poaching is a serious problem for the Venus flytrap and some Nepenthes species.
Never dig carnivorous plants up from bushland.
Growing them at home.
Carnivorous plants break most gardening rules.
Ordinary potting mix and fertiliser can burn their roots.
Most are grown in peat moss or a substitute mixed with sand or perlite.
Tap water often contains enough dissolved minerals to harm them over time, so use rainwater or distilled water, and many types like to sit in a shallow tray of it.
Most need plenty of bright light.
Resist feeding them pieces of meat, which can rot in the trap, and avoid triggering flytraps for fun, since every closure uses energy.
Outdoors, they usually catch all the insects they need.
Buy plants from reputable nurseries that propagate their own stock, not plants that may have been taken from the wild.
The key idea: Carnivorous plants eat animals mainly to gain nitrogen and phosphorus that their poor soils lack.
Part three. The hidden kingdom of fungi.
The mushroom you see is just the tip of the iceberg.
Below ground, fungi feed forests, recycle the dead and sometimes grow into some of the largest living things on Earth.
Not quite plants.
After autumn rain, mushrooms seem to appear overnight.
It is tempting to see them as odd little plants, but fungi are something else.
They cannot make food from sunlight.
Instead, they release digestive enzymes into their surroundings and absorb the nutrients that are broken down.
Their cell walls are made of chitin, the tough material in insect shells, not plant cellulose.
Genetic studies show fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
The kingdom includes yeasts, moulds, mushrooms, rusts and lichen partners.
Around 150,000 species have been named, but the true total is estimated in the millions, and in Australia most fungi are thought to be undescribed.
The fungus underground.
A mushroom is to a fungus roughly what an apple is to an apple tree: a temporary structure for spreading spores.
The main body of most fungi is the mycelium, a web of microscopic threads called hyphae that spread through soil, wood or leaf litter.
A teaspoon of healthy soil can hold a startling length of them.
Mycelium can grow enormous.
In an Oregon forest, a single honey fungus spreads through the soil across nearly ten square kilometres, and is thought to be thousands of years old.
It is often described as one of the largest living organisms on Earth.
Above ground, you would notice only the occasional clump of honey-coloured mushrooms and some unhealthy trees.
Partners of plants.
Most healthy plants have fungi wrapped around or inside their roots.
These partnerships, mycorrhizas, 'fungus root', are formed by the large majority of land plants.
The fungus's fine threads reach much further than roots, gathering water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen.
In return, the plant gives the fungus sugars from photosynthesis.
Some Australian orchids cannot even germinate without the right fungus.
In 1997 Suzanne Simard and colleagues suggested carbon could move between trees through shared fungal networks, and the 'wood wide web' idea took off.
Networks linking roots are real, but how much they move between trees, and whether it helps, is still debated.
A 2023 review argued the evidence for some popular claims, such as 'mother trees', was weaker than often suggested.
Nature's recyclers.
Without fungi, forests would be buried in their own dead wood.
Wood is hard to digest because it contains lignin, a complex material that stiffens plant cell walls.
Few organisms can break lignin down efficiently, and white rot fungi are among the best.
As fungi, bacteria and small animals break down logs, leaves and dead animals, they release nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients back into the soil.
A rotting log in Australian bushland may look like waste, but it is a busy recycling plant and a home for beetles, frogs, lizards and small mammals.
That is one reason many land managers now leave fallen timber on the ground rather than tidying it away.
Friends, foes and safety.
You probably ate fungi today.
Baker's yeast releases carbon dioxide to make bread rise, and yeasts ferment beer and wine.
Penicillium moulds make the blue veins in some cheeses, and koji mould makes soy sauce, miso and sake.
In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed a Penicillium mould killing bacteria on a dish, which led to penicillin.
Cyclosporine, used to prevent organ rejection, also came from a fungus.
But the chytrid fungus has caused declines in hundreds of frog species worldwide, including in Australia.
The death cap mushroom, introduced and found around Canberra and Melbourne, has caused deaths here, and cooking does not make it safe.
This is general information: never eat wild mushrooms unless an expert has identified them, and if you suspect poisoning, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.
The key idea: Fungi are a kingdom of their own that digest food outside their bodies and are more closely related to animals than to plants.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What are mangroves?
Answer. Salt-tolerant trees and shrubs of tidal coasts.
Question two. Why do carnivorous plants catch animals?
Answer. To get nutrients poor soils lack.
Question three. Which group are fungi more closely related to?
Answer. Animals.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
